newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Confusion grows on deployment of Zaire aid force.
newsitem.headline: Confusion grows on deployment of Zaire aid force.

text.p: The question of U.S. approval stood in the way on Wednesday of a Canadian-led relief force for eastern Zaire, and confusion mounted over how and where it would be deployed.

Highlighting the risk of launching a force without support from both sides in Zaire's month-old war, rebels fired with anti-aircraft batteries and machineguns at a plane flying over the city of Goma, saying they suspected French troops were on board.

Aid agencies, in a far smaller relief operation than foreseen with a multinational force, hoped finally to distribute aid to civilians trapped in Goma after a deal with rebels who took the border town two weeks ago.

"(Tuesday's deal) presumably opens the door for a much accelerated presence of humanitarian organisations in Zaire but there still appear to be issues to be tackled through Kinshasa," said Ben Parker of the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs.
More than a million long-term Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees are cut off from all aid by the conflict between Zairean troops and Tutsi rebels, who hold much of east Zaire.
Thousands are feared to be dying on mountains and in the jungle.

U.N. leaders say the multinational force to bring them food and other aid could move by the weekend. Countries ready to take part, led by Canada and France, say they are ready and waiting but some sort of U.S. involvement is widely seen as essential.
A military-led U.S. assessment force of 40 people was due to arrive in Central Africa on Wednesday but Washington said it was still making up its mind on whether to support the force.
"It's something we're actively considering," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns. Officials and diplomats said a formal U.S. decision could come as early as Wednesday.
But just how to help the refugees and Zairean displaced remains unclear and is one reason for Washington's hesitation.

Zaire, which wants the refugees sent home to its tiny eastern neighbours Rwanda and Burundi, nevertheless insists that the aid should be flown to the west -- which could attract refugees deeper into Zaire -- through the town of Kisangani.
U.N. officials have said an airlift of thousands of tonnes of aid could start before the end of the week using Kisangani as a key base and supported by military planes and helicopters.
Kinshasa says deals with the rebels to bring aid in from Rwanda to rebel-held eastern areas violates its sovereignty.
But aid agencies say that is the most practical route.

Michelle Quintaglie of the U.N.'s World Food Programme said taking aid in via Kisangani, 500 km (300 miles) away through difficult terrain, would be a "logistical nightmare" whereas the eastern route was relatively easy.
"We have everything set up on the eastern side of Zaire. Roads are in good condition. We could move in there within 72 hours with large quantities of food," she told Reuters in Nairobi.
"It is unfeasible for us to consider mounting a huge U.N. operation from Kisangani to feed these people."
France, whose early lead role in the push for action was scuppered by hostility from Rwanda and its allied Zairean rebels, suggested it was likely to bless Canadian leadership.

Asked whether a force could be launched in hours, Cooperation Minister Jacques Godfrain told RMC radio: "That is increasingly likely. In the past few hours, Canada has put itself forward to lead the operations.
"Canada could in fact be a key country in this issue."
Canada says the force would need up to 10,000 troops for about two months before the United Nations would take it over.
France, Spain, Italy, South Africa, Ethiopia and Mali are among 12 countries so far to pledge troops. Britain, like the United States a Security Council member, says it is undecided.
Rwanda and the rebels are against French participation in the international force, accusing Paris of a secret agenda to shore up Zairean authority in the east and help the Hutus.
"If French troops arrive in Goma...we will fire on them and resist them," Commandant Andre Kassasse, the rebel chief in Goma, told reporters after the light plane came under fire.
Among the refugees are thousands of armed Hutus who carried out the 1994 genocide of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda, before fleeing to Zaire.
Rwanda, Zaire and the international community say refugees must go home to Rwanda. But the Hutus either do not want to or are controlled by gunmen fearing death or jail if they go back.
The multinational force is supposed to help repatriate them but cannot force them to go home from the vast Mugunga refugee camp near Goma or from hills and forests where they are hiding.
